lessons.content_en:
Reading assessment evaluates speed, accuracy, critical print size, fluency, comprehension, endurance and working distance. Isolated near acuity does not predict continuous reading. Use standardized print or continuous-text passages at controlled sizes and luminance. Record errors, reading speed, smallest print supporting near-maximum speed, symptoms and preferred posture. Optimize refraction, contrast and illumination before magnification trials. Central scotoma, crowding, reduced contrast and poor tracking may impair fluent reading. Confirm any aid with the patient's own reading material.

Clinical application
Start with the patient's stated goal and habitual correction. Record baseline performance, optimize reversible factors and test one intervention at a time. Use standardized conditions where possible and repeat measurements to assess consistency.

Clinical reasoning
Interpret findings alongside ocular diagnosis, visual field, contrast sensitivity, cognition, motor ability and environment. A chart result alone does not prove functional success. Refer for medical assessment if active disease, unexplained deterioration or urgent symptoms are suspected.

Key points
• Assess real tasks, not charts alone.
• Optimize refraction, contrast and illumination.
• Match the intervention to the patient's abilities and environment.
• Train the patient and reassess functional outcomes.
lessons.content_ar:
نقيّم سرعة القراءة ودقتها وحجم الطباعة الحرج والطلاقة والفهم والتحمل ومسافة العمل. حدة القريب بالحروف المنفردة لا تتنبأ وحدها بالقراءة المتصلة. نسجل الأخطاء والسرعة وأصغر طباعة تحافظ على سرعة قريبة من القصوى والأعراض والوضعية. نصحح الانكسار ونحسن التباين والإضاءة قبل تجربة التكبير. قد تعيق العتمة المركزية والتزاحم وضعف التباين وتتبع السطر القراءة. يجب اختبار الوسيلة بنص يستخدمه المريض فعلياً.

التطبيق السريري
ابدأ بهدف المريض وبالتصحيح المعتاد. سجل الأداء الأساسي، وحسّن العوامل القابلة للتعديل، واختبر تدخلاً واحداً في كل مرة. استخدم ظروفاً معيارية قدر الإمكان وكرر القياس للتأكد من ثبات النتيجة.

التفكير السريري
فسر النتائج مع التشخيص والمجال البصري وحساسية التباين والقدرات المعرفية والحركية والبيئة. نتيجة لوحة الفحص وحدها لا تثبت النجاح الوظيفي. أحِل المريض للتقييم الطبي عند الاشتباه بمرض نشط أو تدهور غير مفسر أو أعراض عاجلة.

نقاط أساسية
• قيّم المهام الحقيقية لا اللوحات وحدها.
• حسّن الانكسار والتباين والإضاءة.
• طابق التدخل مع قدرات المريض وبيئته.
• درّب المريض وأعد تقييم النتائج الوظيفية.

lessons.content_en:
Glare is degradation or discomfort caused by excessive luminance or light scatter; photophobia is abnormal light intolerance. Distinguish discomfort glare from disability glare, which reduces task performance. Ask about sources, settings, onset, pain, redness, headache and effects on daily activities. Examine cornea, tear film, media and retina as indicated. Acute painful photophobia with redness requires prompt medical assessment. Trial environmental changes, brimmed hats, side shields, matte surfaces and filters in real settings. Darker filters are not automatically better because they may reduce useful light.

Clinical application
Start with the patient's stated goal and habitual correction. Record baseline performance, optimize reversible factors and test one intervention at a time. Use standardized conditions where possible and repeat measurements to assess consistency.

Key points
• Assess real tasks, not charts alone.
• Optimize refraction, contrast and illumination.
• Match the intervention to the patient's abilities and environment.
• Train the patient and reassess functional outcomes.

lessons.content_en:
Lighting quality depends on illuminance, luminance, direction, uniformity, contrast, reflections and adaptation. More light is not always better: some patients benefit from task lighting while others experience glare or photophobia. Assess the actual task, working distance, shadows and reflective surfaces. Direct adjustable task lighting onto the material, not into the eyes. Use diffuse ambient lighting for mobility, reduce abrupt luminance transitions and prefer matte finishes. Determine a comfortable effective level by functional trial rather than applying one lux value to everyone.

Clinical application
Start with the patient's stated goal and habitual correction. Record baseline performance, optimize reversible factors and test one intervention at a time. Use standardized conditions where possible and repeat measurements to assess consistency.

• Train the patient and reassess functional outcomes.

lessons.content_en:
Magnification increases apparent angular size or retinal image size. It is task-specific and should be considered after refraction, illumination and contrast are optimized. Methods include relative distance, relative size, angular and electronic magnification. Higher magnification commonly reduces field of view and may shorten working distance. Consider target size, posture, dexterity, field, endurance and task type. Prescribe the lowest effective magnification and train the patient in focusing and scanning. Magnification does not repair retinal damage or restore lost visual field.

Clinical application
Start with the patient's stated goal and habitual correction. Record baseline performance, optimize reversible factors and test one intervention at a time. Use standardized conditions where possible and repeat measurements to assess consistency.

Key points
• Assess real tasks, not charts alone.
• Optimize refraction, contrast and illumination.
• Match the intervention to the patient's abilities and environment.
• Train the patient and reassess functional outcomes.

lessons.content_en:
Relative distance magnification occurs when viewing distance is reduced while target size remains constant. Magnification equals original distance divided by new distance; moving from 40 cm to 20 cm gives approximately 2×. It is simple and cost-free but requires adequate focus, near correction when indicated, illumination and comfortable posture. Very close viewing can cause neck strain, restrict the field and make scanning difficult. Trial the method with the patient's actual task and correction.

Clinical application
Start with the patient's stated goal and habitual correction. Record baseline performance, optimize reversible factors and test one intervention at a time. Use standardized conditions where possible and repeat measurements to assess consistency.

Interpret findings alongside ocular diagnosis, visual field, contrast sensitivity, cognition, motor ability and environment. A chart result alone does not prove functional success. Refer for medical assessment if active disease, unexplained deterioration or urgent symptoms are suspected.

Key points
• Assess real tasks, not charts alone.
• Optimize refraction, contrast and illumination.
• Match the intervention to the patient's abilities and environment.
• Train the patient and reassess functional outcomes.

lessons.content_en:
Relative size magnification enlarges the physical target while viewing distance remains unchanged. Magnification is enlarged linear size divided by original size; doubling print dimensions gives 2×. Examples include large-print books, enlarged labels and digital text. It can support comfortable sustained reading without a close working distance, but enlarged material occupies more space and may require scrolling or page turning. Check character quality, contrast and line length after enlargement.

Clinical application
Start with the patient's stated goal and habitual correction. Record baseline performance, optimize reversible factors and test one intervention at a time. Use standardized conditions where possible and repeat measurements to assess consistency.

• Train the patient and reassess functional outcomes.

lessons.content_en:
Angular magnification is the ratio of the visual angle through an optical system to the visual angle without it under defined conditions. Magnifiers and telescopes increase apparent angular size. Practical benefit depends on power, focal distance, eye position, alignment and residual vision. Higher magnification generally narrows the field and increases positioning demands. Teach focusing and alignment, then verify functional gain during the intended task; nominal device power does not guarantee equivalent reading improvement.

Clinical application
Start with the patient's stated goal and habitual correction. Record baseline performance, optimize reversible factors and test one intervention at a time. Use standardized conditions where possible and repeat measurements to assess consistency.

Clinical reasoning
Interpret findings alongside ocular diagnosis, visual field, contrast sensitivity, cognition, motor ability and environment. A chart result alone does not prove functional success. Refer for medical assessment if active disease, unexplained deterioration or urgent symptoms are suspected.

Key points
• Assess real tasks, not charts alone.
• Optimize refraction, contrast and illumination.
• Match the intervention to the patient's abilities and environment.
• Train the patient and reassess functional outcomes.
lessons.content_ar:
التكبير الزاوي هو نسبة الزاوية البصرية عبر النظام إلى الزاوية دون النظام وفق شروط محددة. تزيد المكبرات والمناظير الحجم الزاوي الظاهري. تعتمد الفائدة على القوة والمسافة البؤرية وموضع العين والمحاذاة والرؤية المتبقية. زيادة التكبير تضيق المجال غالباً وتزيد متطلبات التموضع. نعلم التركيز والمحاذاة ثم نقيس الفائدة في المهمة؛ فالرقم الاسمي لا يضمن تحسناً مماثلاً في القراءة.

التطبيق السريري
ابدأ بهدف المريض وبالتصحيح المعتاد. سجل الأداء الأساسي، وحسّن العوامل القابلة للتعديل، واختبر تدخلاً واحداً في كل مرة. استخدم ظروفاً معيارية قدر الإمكان وكرر القياس للتأكد من ثبات النتيجة.

lessons.content_en:
Near dioptric demand is approximately the reciprocal of working distance in metres: 25 cm is 4 D, 20 cm is 5 D and 10 cm is 10 D. Shorter working distances increase accommodative demand and may require a stronger near addition depending on age, residual accommodation and refractive correction. These calculations guide assessment but do not constitute a complete prescription. Consider binocular status, field, posture, lens design and tolerance, then verify clarity and reading performance.

Clinical application
Start with the patient's stated goal and habitual correction. Record baseline performance, optimize reversible factors and test one intervention at a time. Use standardized conditions where possible and repeat measurements to assess consistency.

Clinical reasoning
Interpret findings alongside ocular diagnosis, visual field, contrast sensitivity, cognition, motor ability and environment. A chart result alone does not prove functional success. Refer for medical assessment if active disease, unexplained deterioration or urgent symptoms are suspected.

Key points
• Assess real tasks, not charts alone.
• Optimize refraction, contrast and illumination.
• Match the intervention to the patient's abilities and environment.
• Train the patient and reassess functional outcomes.

lessons.content_en:
Optical low-vision aids include hand and stand magnifiers, high-add spectacles and telescopes. Selection follows functional assessment and considers task distance, required magnification, field, working distance, posture, dexterity, lighting, binocular status and cost. Hand magnifiers are portable but require focusing control. Stand magnifiers stabilize lens-to-task distance but constrain working distance and field. High-add spectacles are hands-free but require close work. Telescopes assist distance spotting and usually require training. Demonstrate and verify benefit with real tasks.

Clinical application
Start with the patient's stated goal and habitual correction. Record baseline performance, optimize reversible factors and test one intervention at a time. Use standardized conditions where possible and repeat measurements to assess consistency.

Clinical reasoning

Key points
• Assess real tasks, not charts alone.
• Optimize refraction, contrast and illumination.
• Match the intervention to the patient's abilities and environment.
• Train the patient and reassess functional outcomes.

lessons.content_en:
Handheld magnifiers are portable aids for near tasks such as labels, menus and brief reading. The target must be placed at the appropriate focal distance. Higher-power lenses generally have shorter focal lengths and smaller fields. Built-in illumination may help some users but can create glare or reflections. Assess hand stability, tremor, dexterity, posture and ability to locate focus. Train the patient to position the magnifier and material correctly and scan systematically. Verify performance using the patient's own reading material.

Clinical application
Start with the patient's stated goal and habitual correction. Record baseline performance, optimize reversible factors and test one intervention at a time. Use standardized conditions where possible and repeat measurements to assess consistency.

Clinical reasoning
Interpret findings alongside ocular diagnosis, visual field, contrast sensitivity, cognition, motor ability and environment. A chart result alone does not prove functional success. Refer for medical assessment if active disease, unexplained deterioration or urgent symptoms are suspected.

Key points
• Assess real tasks, not charts alone.
• Optimize refraction, contrast and illumination.
• Match the intervention to the patient's abilities and environment.
• Train the patient and reassess functional outcomes.
